meta.title: How Teach turns code into a learning module
meta.subject: Teach
meta.one_liner: Two separate agents turn a finished build into one evidence-backed lesson on your computer.
meta.learning_goal: By the end, you can explain what Teach investigates, what passes between its two agents, and how that becomes a local page.

story.title: Working code is not the same as understanding it
story.plain: A build conversation mixes the real system with abandoned ideas, small fixes, and implementation noise. When one prompt tries to inspect all of that and teach it at the same time, it can produce a smooth explanation without a trustworthy mental model.
story.takeaway: Teach first separates confirmed facts from the noise around them.

story.title: Investigation and teaching are now separate jobs
story.plain: The Build Investigator establishes what the code does and removes irrelevant detail. The Learning Designer receives that checked map and decides what an 18-year-old should learn, which example will help, and how to diagram the system.
story.takeaway: The lesson is designed from verified evidence instead of generated directly from a messy conversation.

example.before: One agent reads the build and immediately writes a polished product explanation.
example.after: One agent produces an evidence map; a different agent turns that map into a learning goal, worked example, system diagram, and recall check.
example.insight: Separating truth-finding from teaching makes both jobs easier to inspect and improve.

story.title: Evidence moves through five clear steps
story.plain: Each step has one owner. The labels show whether the work happens in the Teach orchestrator, the investigator, the learning designer, or the local output tools.
story.takeaway: Teach generates and stores the finished lesson locally. It does not publish or host the page.

visual.title: From finished build to learning module

steps.label: Run Teach
steps.detail: The Teach orchestrator creates one output folder and starts the evidence-first workflow.

steps.label: Map the build
steps.detail: The Build Investigator follows the conversation and code, identifies the real system areas, and removes technologies that do not matter to the lesson.

technology.name: JSON
technology.explanation: JSON is the structured text file that carries confirmed facts and their evidence to the next agent.

steps.label: Design the lesson
steps.detail: The Learning Designer sees the validated map—not the noisy source material—and chooses what the learner should understand and remember.

steps.label: Check and render
steps.detail: A deterministic script rejects unsupported evidence, incorrect system labels, or malformed lesson data before building the page.

technology.name: Python
technology.explanation: Python performs the repeatable checks and places the approved lesson inside the page design.

steps.label: Open locally
steps.detail: The browser displays the completed module from a local-only server on the builder's computer.

technology.name: HTML
technology.explanation: HTML is the finished page file that holds the explanation, diagram, and interaction the browser displays.

check.question: Why does the Learning Designer receive a build map instead of reading the entire codebase and conversation again?
check.answer: The build map gives it the confirmed facts, relevant technologies, system boundaries, and evidence without mixing teaching decisions back into code investigation.
check.why: That separation is the core reason Teach can be both accurate and useful for learning.
